cards.front: In the yearly count model for a local population, N_next = {{c1::λ·N + I}}, where λ is the factor its own births and deaths produce and I is immigrants.
cards.quote: Next year's count is this year's multiplied by λ (lambda), the factor its own births and deaths produce that year, plus any immigrants, I: N_next = λ·N + I.

cards.front: In the λ bookkeeping, what defines a species' niche?
cards.back: The set of conditions in which the long-run λ, taken across good and bad years with no immigrants, is at least 1.
cards.quote: A species' niche is the set of conditions in which the long-run λ, taken across good and bad years with no immigrants, is at least 1.

cards.front: A range map differs from a species' niche in two ways. What are the two mismatches?
cards.back: Suitable places the species never reached (empty though conditions are good), and places outside the niche where immigrants keep a population going.
cards.quote: A map adds two mismatches: suitable places never reached, and places outside the niche where immigrants keep a population going.

cards.front: λ, the {{c1::finite rate of increase}}, sums up survival, growth and reproduction across the whole life cycle.
cards.quote: λ, the finite rate of increase, sums up survival, growth and reproduction across the whole life cycle, the vital rates from life histories.

cards.front: A plant population has λ = 0.6 every year, and 12 new plants arrive each year from elsewhere. Where does the count level off?
cards.back: It levels off where losses match arrivals: N = I / (1 − λ) = 12 / (1 − 0.6) = 30 plants, present in every survey.
cards.why: λ below 1 means deaths exceed births, so this is a sink population kept going by immigrants.
cards.quote: the count levels off where losses match arrivals, at 20 / (1 − 0.8) = 100 plants, present in every survey.

cards.front: A plant population holds steady at 100 plants with λ = 0.8 and 20 immigrants a year. The arrivals are cut off. What happens and why?
cards.back: It falls toward zero. With I = 0, each year multiplies the count by 0.8, so nothing replaces the losses.
cards.quote: Cut off the arrivals and it falls toward zero.

cards.front: In Hutchinson's form, a niche with n axes (temperature, soil moisture, salt, food size) is an {{c1::n-dimensional hypervolume}} in niche space, while geographic space is the map.
cards.quote: it is an n-dimensional hypervolume in niche space, while geographic space is the map.

cards.front: Why can one patch of niche space map onto scattered places in geographic space?
cards.back: Conditions vary with latitude, altitude and microclimate, so the same conditions recur in separate places, and one place can hold several microclimates.
cards.quote: Conditions vary with latitude, altitude and microclimate (climate and biomes), so one patch of niche space can map onto scattered places, and one place can hold several microclimates.

cards.front: Why can presence or absence on a range map not, by itself, mark where a species' niche ends?
cards.back: A sink population (λ below 1, kept by immigrants) shows as presence, and a suitable place never reached (N = 0, I = 0) shows as absence.
cards.quote: A map adds two mismatches: suitable places never reached, and places outside the niche where immigrants keep a population going.

cards.front: The {{c1::fundamental}} niche is the set of conditions in which a species can persist with no competitors or enemies present.
cards.quote: The fundamental niche is the set of conditions in which a species can persist with no competitors or enemies present

cards.front: The {{c1::realized}} niche is the set of conditions a species occupies when other species are present.
cards.quote: The realized niche is the set of conditions it occupies when other species are present.

cards.front: How do competitors and enemies, versus helpers, usually change the realized niche relative to the fundamental niche?
cards.back: Competitors and enemies lower λ and usually shrink it to a smaller part of the fundamental niche; helpers raise λ and can extend it past the fundamental niche.
cards.quote: Competitors and enemies usually make it a smaller part of the fundamental niche; helpers can extend it past it.

cards.front: On the rocky shore at Millport, Chthamalus larvae settle below the adult band, but adults live only above Balanus. What experiment separates low-shore conditions from competition with Balanus, and what did it show?
cards.back: Keep Balanus off some lower rock patches and leave it on others. Chthamalus survived low where Balanus was removed, so a competitor left the lower part of its fundamental niche unoccupied.
cards.quote: keep Balanus off some patches of lower rock and leave it on others.

cards.front: On the Millport shore, what did Connell attribute the upper limits of the barnacles to?
cards.back: Mainly heat and drying, with Chthamalus the more tolerant of the two.
cards.quote: Connell attributed the upper limits mainly to heat and drying, with Chthamalus the more tolerant

cards.front: Desert cactus seedlings die in open ground at a site but survive, grow and reproduce under shading nurse shrubs there. If the fundamental niche is defined before any interaction, what does the shrub do to the cactus niche?
cards.back: The realized niche reaches past the fundamental niche. The helper raises λ and lets the cactus persist in conditions it cannot tolerate alone.
cards.why: So 'the realized niche is always smaller' has exceptions, a framing some ecologists dispute.
cards.quote: A shrub that shades seedlings, or a mussel bed that holds water at low tide, raises λ and can let a species persist in conditions it cannot tolerate alone.

cards.front: A species distribution model is fitted to the climates of places where a species has been recorded. What does it describe?
cards.back: The map, sinks and gaps included: occupied conditions plus accessibility, closer to the realized niche filtered by dispersal than to the fundamental niche.
cards.quote: describe the map, sinks and gaps included: occupied conditions plus accessibility, closer to the realized niche filtered by dispersal than to the fundamental niche.

cards.front: How is a thermal performance curve obtained?
cards.back: By rearing individuals in the laboratory at several constant temperatures and recording a named response, such as development rate or survival.
cards.quote: Rearing individuals in the laboratory at several constant temperatures and recording a named response gives a thermal performance curve.
cards.section: Tolerance: one piece of λ at a time

cards.front: On a thermal performance curve for a rate such as development, the rate rises from zero at Tmin, peaks at {{c1::Topt}} and falls to zero at Tmax.
cards.quote: For a rate such as development, it rises from zero at Tmin, peaks at Topt and falls to zero at Tmax
cards.section: Tolerance: one piece of λ at a time

cards.front: A thermal performance curve for larval development rate in a beetle has Tmin = 12 degrees C. A student concludes the larvae die below 12 degrees C. What is wrong?
cards.back: Tmin here is where development rate reaches zero, not necessarily a lethal temperature. Each value belongs to its named response; survival needs its own curve.
cards.quote: Every value belongs to its response: for development, Tmin and Tmax are where that rate reaches zero, not necessarily lethal temperatures.
cards.section: Tolerance: one piece of λ at a time

cards.front: If development to adulthood stops at some temperature, why is λ below 1 there regardless of survival or fecundity?
cards.back: Every individual must pass through that step, so the life cycle cannot be completed and the population cannot replace itself.
cards.quote: the life cycle cannot be completed there and λ is below 1 whatever the other rates do.
cards.section: Tolerance: one piece of λ at a time

cards.front: Across laboratory data sets for moths and butterflies, which rate generally limits performance at the cold end, and which at the hot end?
cards.back: Development rate generally limits the cold end; survival limits the hot end. Different vital rates set the two ends of the tolerance interval.
cards.quote: development rate generally limited performance at the cold end and survival at the hot end.
cards.section: Tolerance: one piece of λ at a time

cards.front: Moth larvae are reared at 14 and 20 degrees C. At 14, standardized survival is 0.95 and standardized development rate 0.15; at 20, survival is 0.90 and development 0.60. Which rate limits combined performance at the cold end, and why?
cards.back: Development rate. Survival stays high, but development is slow, so the product of the two is held down by development.
cards.quote: At 20 degrees C survival is high and development slow, so development limits the cold end.
cards.section: Worked problem: a performance breadth from development and survival

cards.front: Why is a moth's laboratory thermal breadth not the same as its range boundary?
cards.back: In the field it can shelter in shade, and its distribution also depends on host plants, enemies and dispersal. A chamber measures only one piece of λ.
cards.quote: A laboratory breadth is not a range boundary: a moth in the field can shelter in shade, and its distribution also depends on host plants, enemies and dispersal.
cards.section: Tolerance: one piece of λ at a time

cards.front: Combined thermal performance in the Lepidoptera synthesis is P = {{c1::D x S}}, development rate times survival, each scaled to its own maximum.
cards.quote: (D = development rate, S = survival, each scaled to its own maximum)
cards.section: Worked problem: a performance breadth from development and survival

cards.front: A moth is reared at 18, 24 and 30 degrees C. Scaled development D = 0.40, 1.00, 0.90; scaled survival S = 0.90, 0.70, 0.30. Compute P = D x S at each and the best tested temperature.
cards.back: P = 0.40 x 0.90 = 0.36 at 18; 1.00 x 0.70 = 0.70 at 24; 0.90 x 0.30 = 0.27 at 30. Best tested temperature: 24 degrees C (the true peak could lie between treatments).
cards.quote: The best tested temperature is 25 degrees C. The true peak could lie between treatments.
cards.section: Worked problem: a performance breadth from development and survival

cards.front: A moth's combined performance P is 0.36 at 18, 0.70 at 24 and 0.27 at 30 degrees C. Assuming P changes in a straight line between treatments, find the breadth where P is at least 0.50.
cards.why: Interpolate only between treatments; do not extrapolate past 18 or 30 degrees C.
cards.quote: Assume P changes in a straight line between treatments, do not extrapolate beyond 20 or 30 degrees C, and call the acceptable range P of at least 0.50
cards.section: Worked problem: a performance breadth from development and survival

cards.front: Why is a performance breadth from P = D x S neither λ nor a range boundary?
cards.back: P leaves out fecundity, so it is not λ. Its crossings are threshold choices, not lethal limits, and a field range also depends on shelter, other species and dispersal.
cards.quote: P leaves out fecundity, so it is not lambda.
cards.section: Worked problem: a performance breadth from development and survival

cards.front: Two monkeyflowers, Mimulus cardinalis (low elevations) and M. lewisii (high), had near-zero fitness when grown beyond their elevation ranges. Why can this not show that temperature sets the limits?
cards.back: It fits niche limits, but elevation changes many conditions at once, so temperature cannot be separated from the rest.
cards.quote: but elevation changes many conditions at once, so temperature cannot be separated from the rest.

cards.front: In a 2014 meta-analysis of 111 transplant tests beyond species' ranges, in about what share did the range limit sit at a niche limit, and in what share did transplants sustain themselves beyond the range?
cards.back: About 46% at a niche limit; about 26% self-sustaining beyond the range, consistent with dispersal limitation.
cards.quote: In 46% of tests the range limit sat at a niche limit.

cards.front: A plant is recorded every year at its upper elevation edge, but transplants fail even at sites just inside the edge. Using N_next = λ·N + I, interpret the edge.
cards.back: The range runs past the niche limit: edge populations are sinks, with λ below 1 kept going by I above 0.
cards.why: The 2014 review found this in 23% of tests, all at elevation limits.
cards.quote: A range that runs past the niche limit, its edge populations sinks (λ below 1, I above 0).

cards.front: A dune plant planted beyond its range edge exactly triples in 12 years. What average yearly multiplier is that, and what does it show?
cards.back: 3^(1/12) ≈ 1.10 a year. A species can sit just above replacement beyond its edge and still be missing there.
cards.why: A rough illustration, not a measured long-run λ.
cards.quote: Exactly tripling in that time means multiplying by about 1.08 to 1.10 a year on average

cards.front: At the Camissoniopsis dune edge, colonisation of empty patches falls toward the limit. What alternative to 'seeds never arrive' does this suggest?
cards.back: The edge may be held by a balance of colonisation and local extinction: empty patches are colonised more slowly than occupied ones die out.
cards.quote: the edge may be held by a balance of colonisation and local extinction (empty patches colonised more slowly than occupied ones die out)

cards.front: In a beyond-range transplant, why use seed from several source populations, including from the range edge itself?
cards.back: So no one population decides the result, and seed and sites from the range edge itself are included, as the 2014 review stressed.
cards.quote: Seed from several source populations, so no one population decides the result

cards.front: A shrub is planted beyond its northern range edge and at interior sites. Long-run λ beyond the edge is 1.15 with neighbours and 1.25 with neighbours removed. What most likely limits the range?
cards.back: Likely access: dispersal or recolonisation. Populations replace themselves beyond the edge with or without neighbours, so the conditions there lie inside the niche.
cards.quote: transplants sustained themselves beyond the range, consistent with dispersal limitation

cards.front: A beyond-edge transplant gives long-run λ of 0.70 with neighbours and 0.75 with neighbours removed; interior controls give 1.10. A student concludes 'the edge is set by climate.' Evaluate the conclusion.
cards.back: Too strong. Conditions beyond the edge are implicated, and climate is a strong candidate, but herbivores, pathogens or missing soil partners need their own tests first.
cards.why: Rule: λ below 1 with and without neighbours, with interior controls at least 1, implicates conditions, not neighbours or access.
cards.quote: climate is a strong candidate, but herbivores, pathogens or missing soil partners need their own tests before the limit is called abiotic

cards.front: λ alternates between 1.5 in good years and 0.6 in bad ones, averaging 1.05. Why does the population still shrink?
cards.back: Growth multiplies, so each pair of years gives 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9. Long-run λ is the geometric mean, √0.9 ≈ 0.95, below 1.
cards.quote: Each pair of years multiplies it by 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9
cards.section: Why λ has to be a long-run rate

cards.front: A single population's λ alternates between 1.4 and 0.7 each year. Find the arithmetic mean and the long-run λ, and say whether it persists without immigrants.
cards.back: Arithmetic mean = 1.05. Each pair multiplies by 1.4 x 0.7 = 0.98, so long-run λ = √0.98 ≈ 0.99, below 1: it declines slowly and does not persist.
cards.quote: for a single count like this the long-run λ is the geometric mean
cards.section: Why λ has to be a long-run rate

cards.front: A three-year transplant beyond a range edge gives λ = 1.1 every year. Give two reasons the edge could still be a niche limit.
cards.back: A rare lethal year can be missed: λ = 1.1 for nine years and 0.3 in the tenth gives long-run λ about 0.97. A few years at a few sites also misses long-term adaptation at the edge.
cards.why: Rests on long-run λ being the geometric mean across good and bad years.
cards.quote: Most transplants run a few years at a few sites, so rare lethal years and long-term adaptation at the edge are hard to capture.
cards.section: Why λ has to be a long-run rate

cards.front: What is assumed present when a species' fundamental niche is defined?
cards.back: Its food and any partner it cannot live without. The niche is usually drawn on physical conditions and resources.
cards.quote: In the fundamental niche, the species' food and any partner it cannot live without are assumed present.
cards.section: Fine print on the fundamental niche

cards.front: In the Welk study, 14 grassland species grew in nine botanical gardens with a competitor grass sown or not and molluscs excluded or not. Why is competition's effect causal but the precipitation effect on survival only an association?
cards.back: Competitor presence was assigned in a fully crossed design; precipitation varied among gardens rather than being assigned at random, so other garden differences could explain it.
cards.quote: climate varied among gardens rather than being assigned at random, so that part is an association.
cards.section: Field experiment on competition: the Welk study

cards.front: A species' range runs past its niche limit into sink populations, and suitable habitat beyond its other edge has never been reached. How will a species distribution model fitted to its records misjudge its niche?
cards.back: It will include the sink conditions, where λ is below 1, and miss the unreached suitable conditions, because it describes the map, not where λ is at least 1.
cards.why: Rule: the model fits occupied conditions plus accessibility, sinks and gaps included.
cards.quote: Species distribution models, fitted to the climates of places where a species has been recorded, describe the map

cards.front: Design a field test of whether a nurse shrub extends a desert plant's niche into hotter, drier sites than it can tolerate alone.
cards.back: At sites in those conditions, plant seedlings in open ground and under shrubs, with interior controls; estimate long-run λ over several years. λ at least 1 only under shrubs shows the helper extends the realized niche.
cards.why: Rests on helpers raising λ and on long-run λ of at least 1 defining persistence.
cards.quote: If the fundamental niche is defined before any interaction, the realized niche then reaches past the fundamental one

cards.front: A moth's laboratory thermal breadth extends 3 degrees C warmer than its warmest recorded site. Is the range edge set by heat tolerance? What would decide it?
cards.back: Not necessarily: the lab measures one piece of λ, and host plants, enemies and dispersal also shape the range. Plant populations beyond the edge, with interior controls, and estimate long-run λ.
cards.quote: A chamber measures one piece of λ; to learn whether a whole population can replace itself past an edge, you have to plant it there
cards.section: Tolerance: one piece of λ at a time
